claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on emotional prosody recognition.

claims.claim: Individuals with amusia cannot recognize emotions in short samples such as isolated vowels.
claims.source: As for emotional prosody in speech, individuals with amusia can recognize emotions in spoken sentences, but not in short samples such as isolated vowels (Pralus et al., 2019), or when speech has been filtered to remove high-frequency non-pitch cues (Lolli et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to research on emotional prosody perception.

claims.claim: Individuals with amusia cannot recognize emotions when speech has been filtered to remove high-frequency non-pitch cues.
claims.source: As for emotional prosody in speech, individuals with amusia can recognize emotions in spoken sentences, but not in short samples such as isolated vowels (Pralus et al., 2019), or when speech has been filtered to remove high-frequency non-pitch cues (Lolli et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a filtered speech study.

claims.claim: It is unknown how decreased reliance on a particular acoustic cue during speech perception is reflected in the brain.
claims.source: It is unknown how decreased reliance on a particular acoustic cue during speech perception (such as pitch cues in amusia) is reflected in the brain.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: In the 'weighted connections' model of multisensory integration, the relative reliability of the modalities involved with perception of a stimulus is related to differential connectivity strength.
claims.source: In this model, the relative reliability of the modalities involved with perception of a stimulus is related to differential connectivity strength (Beauchamp et al., 2010; Rohe and Noppeney, 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes a theoretical model from the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: When visual information is degraded, the connection strength between lateral occipital cortex and intraparietal sulcus decreases.
claims.source: More concretely, when visual information is degraded, the connection strength between lateral occipital cortex (a visual area) and intraparietal sulcus (a multimodal area) decreases, and when tactile perception is made noisier, connection strength between secondary somatosensory cortex and intraparietal sulcus becomes weaker (Beauchamp et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited multisensory integration study.

claims.claim: When tactile perception is made noisier, connection strength between secondary somatosensory cortex and intraparietal sulcus becomes weaker.
claims.source: More concretely, when visual information is degraded, the connection strength between lateral occipital cortex (a visual area) and intraparietal sulcus (a multimodal area) decreases, and when tactile perception is made noisier, connection strength between secondary somatosensory cortex and intraparietal sulcus becomes weaker (Beauchamp et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited multisensory integration study.

claims.claim: Connection strength between auditory cortex and the STS is weaker when noise has been introduced to the auditory speech.
claims.source: Similarly, effective connectivity between the (multimodal) superior temporal sulcus (STS) and visual and auditory areas has shown similar modulations during processing of audiovisual speech: connection strength between auditory cortex and the STS is weaker when noise has been introduced to the auditory speech, and conversely connection strength between visual cortex and STS is weaker if visual noise is introduced (Nath and Beauchamp, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited audiovisual speech study.

claims.claim: Connection strength between visual cortex and STS is weaker if visual noise is introduced.
claims.source: Similarly, effective connectivity between the (multimodal) superior temporal sulcus (STS) and visual and auditory areas has shown similar modulations during processing of audiovisual speech: connection strength between auditory cortex and the STS is weaker when noise has been introduced to the auditory speech, and conversely connection strength between visual cortex and STS is weaker if visual noise is introduced (Nath and Beauchamp, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited audiovisual speech study.

claims.claim: The acoustic speech signal carries multiple co-occurring acoustic dimensions (e.g. voice pitch, duration, and amplitude), which often provide redundant cues to disambiguate a linguistic category.
claims.source: As mentioned, the acoustic speech signal carries multiple co-occurring acoustic dimensions (e.g. roughly described as voice pitch, duration, and amplitude), which often provide redundant cues to disambiguate a linguistic category (Patel, 2014; Winter, 2014; Jasmin et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about speech acoustics supported by citations to the literature.

claims.claim: Individuals with typical pitch perception have learned through a lifetime of experience with speech acoustics that vocal pitch is a useful and reliable cue.
claims.source: Individuals with typical pitch perception have learned through a lifetime of experience with speech acoustics that vocal pitch is a useful and reliable cue.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about perceptual learning in typical individuals based on general principles.

claims.claim: Individuals with amusia would have learned that, for them, pitch is not a reliable cue for processing spoken language.
claims.source: By contrast, individuals with amusia, who have unreliable perception of and memory for pitch (analogous to the 'noise' introduced in the multisensory integration studies cited above), would have learned that, for them, pitch is not a reliable cue for processing spoken language.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about perceptual learning in individuals with amusia based on their pitch processing difficulties.

claims.claim: Amusics may exhibit decreased connectivity between language regions and pitch-related areas during speech processing.
claims.source: Thus, by analogy to the multisensory weighting results described above, we hypothesize that amusics may exhibit decreased connectivity between language regions and pitch-related areas during speech processing.
claims.evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, based on inference from multisensory integration literature.

claims.claim: The neural foundations of perceptual weighting in speech have not been investigated in atypical individuals.
claims.source: The neural foundations of perceptual weighting in speech have thus far not been investigated in atypical individuals.
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: Only one previous functional neuroimaging study has examined the neural processing of spoken material in people with amusia.
claims.source: Indeed, only one previous functional neuroimaging study has examined the neural processing of spoken material in people with amusia.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on knowledge of previous studies.

claims.claim: In the Albouy et al. 2019 study, no group differences were detected in task-related activation or functional connectivity during processing of speech.
claims.source: In this study, no group differences were detected in task-related activation or functional connectivity during processing of speech (whereas group differences were observed during processing of tones; Albouy et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited previous study.

claims.claim: In the Albouy et al. 2019 study, group differences were observed during processing of tones.
claims.source: In this study, no group differences were detected in task-related activation or functional connectivity during processing of speech (whereas group differences were observed during processing of tones; Albouy et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim describes findings from a cited previous study.

claims.claim: The connectivity analyses in the Albouy et al. 2019 study focused on the silent retention interval in a task in which participants needed to maintain phonemic and not pitch-related information in memory.
claims.source: However, the connectivity analyses in this study focused on the silent retention interval in a task in which participants needed to maintain phonemic and not pitch-related information in memory; the analyses also used broader bilateral ROIs within networks associated with language processing.
claims.evidence: This describes methodological details of a cited previous study.

claims.claim: The Albouy et al. 2019 study used broader bilateral ROIs within networks associated with language processing.
claims.source: However, the connectivity analyses in this study focused on the silent retention interval in a task in which participants needed to maintain phonemic and not pitch-related information in memory; the analyses also used broader bilateral ROIs within networks associated with language processing.
claims.evidence: This describes methodological details of a cited previous study.

claims.claim: It remains an open question how functional connectivity in amusic and non-amusic participants may differ during speech encoding in pitch-related language tasks within regions of interest selected with a whole-brain data-driven approach.
claims.source: It remains an open question how functional connectivity in amusic and non-amusic participants may differ during speech encoding in pitch-related language tasks within regions of interest selected with a whole-brain data-driven approach.
claims.evidence: This identifies the specific research question addressed by the current study.

claims.claim: The study scanned 15 individuals with amusia and 15 controls using functional magnetic resonance imaging.
claims.source: To determine whether the relative reliability of auditory dimensions in speech perception is reflected in functional connectivity, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to scan 15 individuals with amusia and 15 controls.
claims.evidence: This describes the sample size and methodology of the current study.

claims.claim: Participants matched spoken sentences with visually presented ones on the basis of the position of intonational phrase boundaries.
claims.source: Participants matched spoken sentences with visually presented ones on the basis of the position of intonational phrase boundaries.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental task used in the study.

claims.claim: In the Pitch-Informative condition, only pitch cues could be used to make the judgment.
claims.source: These intonation changes were conveyed differently, in three conditions: Pitch-Informative (where only pitch cues could be used to make the judgment), Duration-Informative (where only duration cues could be used) or Both-Informative (both pitch and duration cues could be used; Jasmin et al., 2020a; Jasmin et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and conditions.

claims.claim: In the Duration-Informative condition, only duration cues could be used to make the judgment.
claims.source: These intonation changes were conveyed differently, in three conditions: Pitch-Informative (where only pitch cues could be used to make the judgment), Duration-Informative (where only duration cues could be used) or Both-Informative (both pitch and duration cues could be used; Jasmin et al., 2020a; Jasmin et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and conditions.

claims.claim: In the Both-Informative condition, both pitch and duration cues could be used.
claims.source: These intonation changes were conveyed differently, in three conditions: Pitch-Informative (where only pitch cues could be used to make the judgment), Duration-Informative (where only duration cues could be used) or Both-Informative (both pitch and duration cues could be used; Jasmin et al., 2020a; Jasmin et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design and conditions.

claims.claim: Task performance was matched between the groups.
claims.source: Crucially, task performance was matched between the groups (based on prior behavioural testing; Jasmin et al., 2020a), ensuring that any neural differences did not simply represent an inability to perform the task.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design based on prior behavioral data.

claims.claim: Functional connectivity between regions identified in the speech task was compared to functional connectivity calculated from different scanning runs with a passive listening task.
claims.source: Finally, functional connectivity between these areas was analyzed with respect to prosodic cue weights obtained outside the scanner, and also compared to functional connectivity calculated from different scanning runs with a passive listening task.
claims.evidence: This describes an additional analysis performed in the study.

claims.claim: Overall, proportion correct across amusia and control groups was matched.
claims.source: Overall, proportion correct across amusia and control groups was matched (main effect of Group, F(1,84) = 0.16, p=0.69, interaction of Group by Condition, F(2,84) = 0.374, p=0.96).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data collected in the scanner.

claims.claim: The lack of interaction between Group and Condition was predicted based on previous results obtained from a similar paradigm using out-of-scanner data from the same participants.
claims.source: This lack of interaction was predicted based on previous results obtained from a similar paradigm using out-of-scanner data but from the same participants (Jasmin et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This relates the current findings to previous behavioral work.

claims.claim: There was a main effect of condition on performance.
claims.source: There was a main effect of condition (F(2,84) = 3.32, p=0.04).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Performance in the Both-Informative condition was more accurate than in the Pitch-Informative condition.
claims.source: Follow-up post-hoc testing indicated that performance in the Both-Informative condition (with pitch and duration cues simultaneously present) was more accurate than either Pitch-Informative (t(84) = 2.31, p=0.023) or Duration-Informative (t(84) = 2.15, p=0.03), a result that was also predicted and which replicates the behavioral findings in Jasmin et al., 2020a.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc testing of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Performance in the Both-Informative condition was more accurate than in the Duration-Informative condition.
claims.source: Follow-up post-hoc testing indicated that performance in the Both-Informative condition (with pitch and duration cues simultaneously present) was more accurate than either Pitch-Informative (t(84) = 2.31, p=0.023) or Duration-Informative (t(84) = 2.15, p=0.03), a result that was also predicted and which replicates the behavioral findings in Jasmin et al., 2020a.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc testing of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: The finding that performance in the Both-Informative condition was more accurate replicates the behavioral findings in Jasmin et al., 2020a.
claims.source: Follow-up post-hoc testing indicated that performance in the Both-Informative condition (with pitch and duration cues simultaneously present) was more accurate than either Pitch-Informative (t(84) = 2.31, p=0.023) or Duration-Informative (t(84) = 2.15, p=0.03), a result that was also predicted and which replicates the behavioral findings in Jasmin et al., 2020a.
claims.evidence: This relates the current findings to previous work.

claims.claim: Comparing whole-brain connectedness values by group revealed four significant locations that showed greater whole-brain connectedness for the control than for the amusia group.
claims.source: Comparing whole-brain connectedness values by group (Amusia vs. Controls) revealed four significant locations (where z of peak vertices > 4.61, FDR-corrected p<0.05) that showed greater whole-brain connectedness for the control than for the amusia group (see Figure 3, yellow crosses).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the neuroimaging analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: All group differences in whole-brain connectedness were located in the inferior frontal cortex.
claims.source: All group differences were located in the inferior frontal cortex: two left hemisphere vertices (inferior frontal gyrus p. triangularis and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) and two right hemisphere vertices (inferior frontal gyrus p. triangularis and p. orbitalis).
claims.evidence: This describes the anatomical locations of the connectivity differences found in the analysis.

claims.claim: There were no areas where whole-brain connectedness differed by Condition.
claims.source: There were no areas where whole-brain connectedness differed by Condition, or showed an interaction of Group and Condition.
claims.evidence: This is a null result from the neuroimaging analysis.

claims.claim: There were no areas where whole-brain connectedness showed an interaction of Group and Condition.
claims.source: There were no areas where whole-brain connectedness differed by Condition, or showed an interaction of Group and Condition.
claims.evidence: This is a null result from the neuroimaging analysis.

claims.claim: Amusic participants' left inferior frontal gyrus seed region showed particularly notable decreases in connectivity with the right posterior superior temporal and inferior parietal cortex.
claims.source: Relative to control participants, amusic participants' left inferior frontal gyrus seed region showed particularly notable decreases in connectivity with the right posterior superior temporal and inferior parietal cortex, as well as with the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Amusic participants' left inferior frontal gyrus seed region showed particularly notable decreases in connectivity with the right posterior superior temporal sulcus.
claims.source: Relative to control participants, amusic participants' left inferior frontal gyrus seed region showed particularly notable decreases in connectivity with the right posterior superior temporal and inferior parietal cortex, as well as with the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: There was weaker connectivity between left inferior frontal gyrus and the right nucleus accumbens in the amusia group.
claims.source: Analysis of subcortical connectivity indicated that there was also weaker connectivity with the right nucleus accumbens (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the subcortical connectivity analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claims.claim: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the mid portions of the right superior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the mid portions of the right superior temporal gyrus, posterior part of the right middle temporal gyrus extending into the inferior bank of the superior temporal sulcus, and the right anterior insula (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the posterior part of the right middle temporal gyrus extending into the inferior bank of the superior temporal sulcus.
claims.source: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the mid portions of the right superior temporal gyrus, posterior part of the right middle temporal gyrus extending into the inferior bank of the superior temporal sulcus, and the right anterior insula (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the right anterior insula.
claims.source: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in amusic participants showed decreased functional connectivity with the mid portions of the right superior temporal gyrus, posterior part of the right middle temporal gyrus extending into the inferior bank of the superior temporal sulcus, and the right anterior insula (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Several subcortical structures showed significantly reduced connectivity with the left DLPFC seed in amusics, including bilateral caudate nucleus and putamen, bilateral pallidum, bilateral cerebellum, and bilateral thalamus.
claims.source: Several subcortical structures - bilateral caudate nucleus and putamen, bilateral pallidum, bilateral cerebellum, and bilateral thalamus - also showed significantly reduced (FDR-corrected) connectivity with the seed in amusics (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the subcortical connectivity analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claims.claim: The right pars triangularis seed showed Control > Amusic connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: The right pars triangularis seed showed Control > Amusic connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The right pars triangularis seed showed Control > Amusic connectivity with left posterior superior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: The right pars triangularis seed showed Control > Amusic connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The right pars triangularis seed showed decreased connectivity with left nucleus accumbens in the amusia group.
claims.source: It also showed decreased connectivity with left nucleus accumbens.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the subcortical connectivity analysis.

claims.claim: Right pars orbitalis showed decreased connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in the amusia group.
claims.source: Right pars orbitalis showed decreased connectivity with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the seed-to-whole-brain connectivity analysis, with reference to Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Right pars orbitalis showed decreased connectivity with the left thalamus in the amusia group.
claims.source: There was also decreased connectivity with the left thalamus (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the subcortical connectivity analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claims.claim: Normalized cue weights were correlated with L-DLPFC <=> R insula connectivity (Spearman R = 0.78, p=0.000037).
claims.source: Across this subset of participants, normalized cue weights were correlated with L-DLPFC <=> R insula connectivity (Spearman R = 0.78, p=0.000037), and L-DLPFC <=> R auditory cortex connectivity (Spearman R = 0.75, p=0.000154; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 4.

claims.claim: Normalized cue weights were correlated with L-DLPFC <=> R auditory cortex connectivity (Spearman R = 0.75, p=0.000154).
claims.source: Across this subset of participants, normalized cue weights were correlated with L-DLPFC <=> R insula connectivity (Spearman R = 0.78, p=0.000037), and L-DLPFC <=> R auditory cortex connectivity (Spearman R = 0.75, p=0.000154; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 4.

claims.claim: Participants who relied least on pitch information to process speech had the weakest functional connectivity between L-DLPFC and right insula/auditory cortex.
claims.source: This indicated that participants who relied least on pitch information to process speech had the weakest functional connectivity between these areas, while those who relied most on pitch had the strongest.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results.

claims.claim: Participants who relied most on pitch had the strongest functional connectivity between L-DLPFC and right insula/auditory cortex.
claims.source: This indicated that participants who relied least on pitch information to process speech had the weakest functional connectivity between these areas, while those who relied most on pitch had the strongest.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results.

claims.claim: During speech perception, amusic subjects showed reduced functional connectivity between left frontal and right insula/auditory ROIs relative to controls.
claims.source: Whereas during speech perception amusic subjects showed reduced functional connectivity between left frontal and right insula/auditory ROIs relative to controls (p=0.0001 for both ROIs; in line with the whole-brain imaging analyses), this pattern did not hold during passive listening to tones (Amusia vs Control connectivity, p=0.29, Group (Amusic, Control) by Task (Speech Perception, Passive Tone Listening) interaction p=0.045 for the insula ROI; Amusia vs Control p=0.30, Group by Task interaction p=0.035 for the auditory cortex ROI - see Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison between speech and tone listening tasks, with reference to Figure 5.

claims.claim: The pattern of reduced connectivity between left frontal and right insula/auditory ROIs in amusics did not hold during passive listening to tones.
claims.source: Whereas during speech perception amusic subjects showed reduced functional connectivity between left frontal and right insula/auditory ROIs relative to controls (p=0.0001 for both ROIs; in line with the whole-brain imaging analyses), this pattern did not hold during passive listening to tones (Amusia vs Control connectivity, p=0.29, Group (Amusic, Control) by Task (Speech Perception, Passive Tone Listening) interaction p=0.045 for the insula ROI; Amusia vs Control p=0.30, Group by Task interaction p=0.035 for the auditory cortex ROI - see Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison between speech and tone listening tasks, with reference to Figure 5.

claims.claim: The Group by Task interactions suggest that the neural connectivity results are specifically linked to speech perception, rather than reflecting an overall connectivity difference between groups regardless of task state.
claims.source: These interactions suggest that our neural connectivity results are specifically linked to speech perception, rather than reflecting an overall connectivity difference between groups regardless of task state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction effects from the task comparison.

claims.claim: No significant differences in activation levels were detected for the main effects of group and condition, nor the interaction of those factors.
claims.source: No significant differences were detected for the main effects of group and condition, nor the interaction of those factors.
claims.evidence: This is a null result from the activation analysis.

claims.claim: Individuals with amusia exhibited decreased functional connectivity between left frontal areas and right hemisphere pitch-related regions.
claims.source: We found that individuals with amusia, who have been previously shown to rely less on pitch than controls to process spoken language (Jasmin et al., 2020a), exhibited decreased functional connectivity between left frontal areas and right hemisphere pitch-related regions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the neuroimaging analysis.

claims.claim: The amusic group exhibited decreased functional connectivity with several sites in frontal, temporal and occipital cortex.
claims.source: Using a data-driven approach, we identified four regions in left and right inferior frontal cortex for which the amusic group exhibited decreased functional connectivity with several other sites in frontal, temporal and occipital cortex.
claims.evidence: This summarizes the findings from the whole-brain connectivity analysis.

claims.claim: The most prominent result was decreased connectivity between left frontal regions classically implicated in language processing (left IFG and DLPFC) and right hemisphere regions in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, and anterior insula.
claims.source: The most prominent of these results was decreased connectivity between left frontal regions classically implicated in language processing (left IFG and DLPFC) and right hemisphere regions —in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, and anterior insula—that have been implicated in pitch processing (Lee et al., 2011; Garcea et al., 2017; Warren et al., 2003; Hohmann et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This summarizes the most prominent finding and relates it to the literature on pitch processing regions.

claims.claim: Right hemisphere regions in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, and anterior insula have been implicated in pitch processing.
claims.source: The most prominent of these results was decreased connectivity between left frontal regions classically implicated in language processing (left IFG and DLPFC) and right hemisphere regions —in the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus, Heschl's gyrus, and anterior insula—that have been implicated in pitch processing (Lee et al., 2011; Garcea et al., 2017; Warren et al., 2003; Hohmann et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the functional role of brain regions based on citations to the literature.

claims.claim: The decreased connectivity between right hemisphere pitch and left hemisphere frontal cortices may relate to the unreliability of the amusics' perception of and memory for pitch.
claims.source: We suggest that this decreased connectivity between right hemisphere pitch and left hemisphere frontal cortices may relate to the unreliability of the amusics' perception of and memory for pitch.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to perceptual reliability.

claims.claim: The decreased connectivity pattern is similar to the 'weighted connections' model of multisensory integration, where a more (or less) reliable modality is given a stronger (or weaker) weight.
claims.source: This is similar to the 'weighted connections' model of multisensory integration, where a more (or less) reliable modality is given a stronger (or weaker) weight (Beauchamp et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This draws an analogy between the current findings and a theoretical model from the literature.

claims.claim: Congenital amusia is often described as a disorder related to structural and functional connectivity within the right hemisphere, particularly between right inferior frontal cortices and right posterior temporal cortex.
claims.source: Congenital amusia is often described as a disorder related to structural and functional connectivity within the right hemisphere, particularly between right inferior frontal cortices and right posterior temporal cortex (see Peretz, 2016 for review).
claims.evidence: This summarizes the prevailing view in the literature, supported by citation to a review.

claims.claim: Right inferior frontal cortex exhibited strongly decreased functional connectivity in the amusia group.
claims.source: Consistent with this proposal, we found in the present study that right inferior frontal cortex exhibited strongly decreased functional connectivity in the amusia group, and follow-up seed testing revealed that right auditory areas were involved as well.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study that is consistent with previous literature.

claims.claim: Sites in left frontal cortex also showed large decreases in connectivity in amusia, most prominently with right hemisphere auditory areas.
claims.source: However, we also found that sites in left frontal cortex also showed large decreases in connectivity in amusia, also most prominently with right hemisphere auditory areas.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study that extends beyond previous literature.

claims.claim: The results are consistent with an account that right hemisphere auditory areas are not only abnormally connected to right frontal areas but are less integrated with frontal left hemisphere regions when processing speech and language.
claims.source: Our results are consistent with an account that right hemisphere auditory areas are not only abnormally connected to right frontal areas (as observed during tonal tasks) but are less integrated with frontal left hemisphere regions when processing speech and language.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings that extends the prevailing theoretical account.

claims.claim: The null results for group differences in activation during speech processing are consistent with prior reports that amusics and controls do not differ in pitch representations within sensory regions.
claims.source: Our null results for group differences in activation during speech processing are consistent with prior reports that amusics and controls do not differ in pitch representations within sensory regions.
claims.evidence: This relates the null activation findings to previous literature.

claims.claim: The extent of pitch-responsive regions within auditory cortex has been shown to be similar in participants with amusia and controls.
claims.source: For example, the extent of pitch-responsive regions within auditory cortex has been shown to be similar in participants with amusia and controls (Norman-Haignere et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citation.

claims.claim: Brainstem encoding of pitch in speech and musical stimuli is unimpaired in individuals with amusia.
claims.source: Brainstem encoding of pitch in speech and musical stimuli is similarly unimpaired in individuals with amusia (Liu et al., 2015b).
claims.evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citation.

claims.claim: In oddball EEG paradigms, amusics show similar pre-attentive mismatch negativity responses to small pitch deviants.
claims.source: Moreover, in oddball EEG paradigms, amusics show similar pre-attentive mismatch negativity responses to small pitch deviants, but impaired attention-dependent P300 responses (Moreau et al., 2009; Peretz et al., 2009; Mignault Goulet et al., 2012; Moreau et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In oddball EEG paradigms, amusics show impaired attention-dependent P300 responses to pitch deviants.
claims.source: Moreover, in oddball EEG paradigms, amusics show similar pre-attentive mismatch negativity responses to small pitch deviants, but impaired attention-dependent P300 responses (Moreau et al., 2009; Peretz et al., 2009; Mignault Goulet et al., 2012; Moreau et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Amusics show intact non-volitional behavioral responses (unconscious pitch shifts) when presented with pitch-altered feedback of their own voice.
claims.source: These findings, along with the fact that amusics show intact non-volitional behavioral responses (unconscious pitch shifts) when presented with pitch-altered feedback of their own voice (Hutchins and Peretz, 2012), have been interpreted as evidence that amusia is a disorder of pitch awareness rather than one of low-level pitch processing (Peretz et al., 2009), with differences in structural connectivity as one possible foundation of this putative impaired pitch awareness (Hyde et al., 2006; Loui et al., 2009; but see Chen et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The findings have been interpreted as evidence that amusia is a disorder of pitch awareness rather than one of low-level pitch processing.

claims.claim: Down-weighting of pitch information during perceptual categorization in both speech and music is adaptive in amusics, inasmuch as they have learned that pitch is an unreliable source of evidence relative to other perceptual dimensions.

results.result: In-scanner behavioral performance was matched between amusia and control groups, with no Group × Condition interaction. Performance was better in the Both-Informative condition compared to single-cue conditions, replicating prior out-of-scanner findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 provide converging statistical evidence (main effects, interactions, post-hoc tests) demonstrating matched performance between groups and a predicted advantage for redundant cues. The replication of prior behavioral work (C50, C54) strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: Whole-brain connectedness analysis identified four regions in inferior frontal cortex showing greater connectivity in controls than amusics. No condition effects or Group × Condition interactions were detected.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 report FDR-corrected whole-brain connectivity results with appropriate statistical thresholds (z > 4.61, p < 0.05). The null findings for condition effects (C57-C58) are clearly stated. The data-driven approach is methodologically sound.

results.result: Seed-to-whole-brain analyses revealed that amusics showed decreased functional connectivity between left frontal seeds (IFG, DLPFC) and right hemisphere auditory/pitch-processing regions (superior temporal gyrus/sulcus, insula), as well as with multiple subcortical structures. Right frontal seeds also showed reduced connectivity patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C70 provide detailed anatomical localization of connectivity differences with FDR correction (p < 0.00035). The findings are visualized in Figure 3 and Table 1. The pattern is internally consistent across multiple seed regions, though the large number of comparisons raises some concern about multiple testing despite FDR correction.

results.result: Functional connectivity between left DLPFC and right auditory regions (insula, auditory cortex) correlated strongly with behavioral cue weights (Spearman R = 0.75-0.78, p < 0.0002). Participants relying more on pitch showed stronger connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 report strong correlations with highly significant p-values and appropriate non-parametric statistics. However, the analysis uses only 21 of 30 participants, and the within-group analyses (mentioned in text) show weaker effects. The correlation is compelling but based on a modest sample size.

results.result: The reduced connectivity between left frontal and right auditory regions in amusics was specific to speech perception and not present during passive tone listening, as evidenced by significant Group × Task interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 provide critical specificity evidence through significant interactions (p = 0.035-0.045) and null effects during the control task. This addresses the important alternative explanation that connectivity differences reflect trait rather than task-related differences. The statistical evidence is adequate though interaction p-values are modest.

results.result: No group or condition differences in activation levels were detected during the speech processing task.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 reports null activation findings that are consistent with prior literature on amusia (C89-C93). While null results require cautious interpretation, the finding aligns with theoretical predictions that amusia involves connectivity rather than activation differences.

results.result: The study's primary finding is that individuals with amusia show reduced functional connectivity between left prefrontal language regions and right hemisphere pitch-processing regions during speech perception, and this connectivity pattern reflects behavioral cue weighting differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 and C79-C81 synthesize the main findings. The convergence of whole-brain connectivity differences (C55-C70), brain-behavior correlations (C71-C74), and task specificity (C75-C77) provides strong support. The integration of multiple analysis approaches strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The authors propose that reduced connectivity reflects an adaptive compensatory mechanism whereby amusics downweight unreliable pitch information, analogous to multisensory integration models where less reliable modalities receive weaker weighting.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C83-C84, C97, C106-C107 present a theoretical interpretation. While the analogy to multisensory integration is reasonable and the data are consistent with this account, the interpretation remains speculative. Alternative explanations (e.g., developmental differences in connectivity) are not fully ruled out. The mechanism is inferred rather than directly tested.

results.result: The authors argue that amusia primarily reflects pitch memory rather than pitch awareness deficits, based on evidence that encoding is intact but working memory demands exacerbate impairments.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C103 present an alternative theoretical account supported by citations to prior work. However, the current study does not directly test memory versus awareness accounts. The argument relies heavily on inference from prior literature and the working memory demands of the task (C99), which are not directly measured. This remains a plausible but unproven hypothesis.

results.result: The authors argue against a purely structural connectivity account of amusia, noting that functional connectivity differences are task-dependent rather than present across all contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 present a logical argument supported by the current data (C75-C77, C105) and prior work (Albouy et al., 2019). The task-specificity of connectivity differences provides evidence against a purely structural account. However, the relationship between structural and functional connectivity is complex and not fully resolved.

results.result: The study used appropriate methods including matched groups (N=15 per group), validated amusia classification (MBEA), and a well-controlled speech perception task with three conditions manipulating pitch and duration cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 and C123-C130 describe methodological details. The sample size is modest but typical for neuroimaging studies of rare conditions. Groups are well-matched on relevant variables (C127-C130). The task design is appropriate and builds on prior validated work. Performance matching (C47) is a strength that controls for task difficulty confounds.

results.result: Stimuli were carefully designed compound sentences with pitch differences (4.0-12.6 semitones) that exceeded even the most impaired participant's detection threshold, avoiding performance confounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 describe stimulus properties with quantitative acoustic measurements. The design ensures that pitch differences are suprathreshold for all participants (C133), which is critical for avoiding confounds. This is a methodological strength that supports valid interpretation of neural differences.

results.result: The study employed beta series correlation analysis, which is reported to be more powerful than alternatives like gPPI for event-related designs.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 describe the connectivity analysis method with appropriate citations. The choice of beta series correlation is justified by prior methodological work (Cisler et al., 2014). However, the claim about superior power (C135) relies on a single citation and may not generalize to all contexts.

results.result: No condition-specific connectivity differences were observed, possibly because the imaging protocol captured responses to the second stimulus when participants could not yet know which cue would be informative, and pitch was suprathreshold in all conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 report null condition effects and provide post-hoc explanations. The null finding is clearly stated (C112), but the explanations (C113-C116) are speculative. The timing argument (C113-C114) is reasonable but not directly tested. Alternative explanations (e.g., insufficient power, inappropriate timing) are not fully explored.

results.result: The introduction establishes that congenital amusia involves unreliable pitch processing, that individuals downweight pitch cues during speech perception, and that the neural basis involves right hemisphere connectivity, though speech perception deficits are subtle in naturalistic contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C24 summarize established knowledge from prior literature with appropriate citations. These background claims are well-supported by the cited work and provide necessary context. The characterization of amusia and its effects on speech perception is consistent with the field's understanding.

results.result: The study addresses a gap in understanding how perceptual cue weighting is reflected in brain connectivity, drawing on multisensory integration models where reliability modulates connectivity strength. Prior neuroimaging of speech in amusia is limited.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C41 establish the rationale and novelty of the study. The gap in the literature is clearly identified (C25, C35-C41), and the theoretical framework from multisensory integration (C26-C30) provides a strong foundation. The hypothesis (C34) follows logically from this framework.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within existing theories of amusia, noting consistency with right hemisphere connectivity accounts while extending to left hemisphere involvement. Null activation findings align with evidence that pitch encoding is intact in amusia.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C96 integrate current findings with prior literature. The discussion appropriately acknowledges both consistency (C85-C86) and novel extensions (C87-C88) of previous work. The interpretation of null activation results (C89-C96) is well-grounded in prior evidence. The synthesis is balanced and scholarly.

results.result: The authors reconcile their findings with a prior study (Hyde et al., 2011) that found different connectivity patterns during passive tone listening, noting methodological differences in seed selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 address an apparent discrepancy in the literature. The reconciliation based on methodological differences (C111) is reasonable, though not definitive. The discussion appropriately acknowledges rather than dismisses the prior work. This demonstrates scholarly rigor in addressing conflicting findings.

results.result: The discussion proposes future directions including experimental manipulation of cue reliability and examination of populations with enhanced pitch perception (tone language speakers, musicians).
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C122 outline reasonable future directions grounded in the current findings and prior literature. The predictions about tone language speakers (C121) follow logically from the current results, though they remain speculative. These suggestions appropriately extend the work without overstating implications.
